summaries.example: Imagine that Maya accidentally knocks over a classmate’s model while carrying books. She did cause the model to fall, so she has causal responsibility. But if she could not have seen the model and did not mean to hurt anyone, blaming her may not be fair. If she knocked it over on purpose because she wanted to ruin it, blame seems more fitting. The difference is not only what happened, but also what Maya knew, wanted, and could control.
summaries.summary: Moral responsibility asks when it is fair to praise or blame someone for an action or its results. It is not the same as causal responsibility: a person may cause an event without deserving blame. Philosophers study the abilities that seem important, such as choosing, understanding reasons, noticing moral concerns, and guiding behavior. They also ask whether freedom is possible if determinism is true. Some philosophers think responsibility practices are useful because praise and blame can influence future behavior. Others say responsibility is mainly about our relationships and emotional responses, such as resentment when someone shows bad will or gratitude when someone helps us with care. Further debates ask whether people are responsible for results, whether luck changes blame, whether personal history matters, and whether ignorance excuses. There is no single agreed answer.
key_ideas: Moral responsibility is different from simply causing something to happen.
People may be praised for good actions and blamed for bad ones, but blame receives more attention in philosophy.
Philosophers disagree about whether responsibility needs the power to have done something else.
Some accounts look to future benefits, while others focus on feelings, relationships, reasons, or fairness.
Accidents, lack of understanding, strong compulsions, and very young age can affect whether blame is appropriate.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas can help us judge people more carefully. They remind us to ask what a person intended, knew, could control, and understood before blaming them. They also show why fairness matters in friendships, families, classrooms, and communities. Thinking about responsibility can help us separate a harmful result from a blameworthy choice and can encourage responses that repair relationships or prevent future harm.

important_terms.definition: Being properly open to praise or blame for what you do, because the action came from your abilities, choices, and understanding in the right way.
Being part of what made something happen. A person can cause an event without being morally blameworthy for it.
The idea that every event is made necessary by earlier events and the laws of nature. Philosophers debate whether this leaves room for freedom.
A response that says someone did something wrong and may deserve criticism or a consequence.
A feeling or response toward someone who has treated you badly, especially when the treatment seems to show a lack of care or respect.

questions_to_think_about: Should someone be blamed for an accident? Why or why not?
Is it enough that a person could have acted differently if they had wanted to?
When should not knowing something excuse a person?
Can a person cause harm without being morally responsible for the harm?

summaries.example: Suppose Alex installs a program that secretly damages a school’s files. Alex knows the program is risky, understands that the files matter, and chooses to run it anyway. A reasons-responsiveness view would ask whether Alex’s decision-making process could recognize and respond to relevant reasons, such as the risk of harm. A reactive-attitudes view would ask whether the act expressed disregard for others and whether resentment or blame is fitting. A forward-looking view might justify criticism partly by its effects on future behavior. If Alex had been hypnotized, compelled, or unaware of the relevant facts in a way that was not Alex’s fault, these judgments could change.
summaries.summary: The entry examines moral responsibility as the status that makes praise, blame, and accountability appropriate. It separates this status from causal responsibility and from responsibility understood as having an obligation. Traditional debates connect responsibility to free will and ask whether the ability to do otherwise is compatible with determinism. Compatibilists argue that responsibility may instead require freedom from coercion, action guided by the agent’s own reasons, or a reasons-responsive mechanism. Frankfurt-style cases challenge the necessity of alternatives, although their interpretation remains disputed. Other approaches justify responsibility through future benefits or explain it through reactive attitudes such as resentment and gratitude, which express concern about another person’s will and regard for others. Contemporary debates refine the subject by distinguishing attribution, accountability, and answerability; discussing moral competence, conversational exchange, standing to blame, and the epistemic condition; and examining outcomes, omissions, luck, personal history, manipulation, and skepticism. The entry presents competing arguments rather than settling all of them.
key_ideas: The central issue is not only whether an agent caused an action, but whether the action arose from the agent’s capacities in the right way.
A major dispute concerns whether responsibility requires genuine access to alternatives or instead requires control over the actual process leading to the action.
Forward-looking theories emphasize useful consequences, while reactive-attitudes theories emphasize interpersonal emotions, expectations, and moral regard.
Some philosophers distinguish attributability, accountability, and answerability: an action may reveal something about a person without yet making blame fair.
Responsibility may depend on moral understanding, personal history, knowledge of consequences, and whether ignorance can be traced to an earlier culpable choice.
Luck creates a challenge because outcomes and even character can depend on factors outside an agent’s control.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory of responsibility affects how we understand blame, praise, punishment, apology, forgiveness, and moral criticism. It encourages a distinction between explaining an action and excusing it, and between recognizing that an action reflects a person and deciding whether accountability is fair. These distinctions matter wherever people evaluate conduct: personal relationships, education, law, and public institutions. They also help us ask whether our responses should focus on desert, communication, repair, protection, moral development, or some combination.

important_terms.definition: A relation to an action or outcome that makes praise or blame appropriate, rather than merely identifying who caused the event.
The view that free will and responsibility cannot exist if determinism is true.
The view that free will and responsibility can exist even if determinism is true, often because the agent acts without external compulsion and from their own choices.
A theory that justifies praise and blame by their useful future effects, such as encouraging better choices or protecting people.
Emotional responses, including resentment and gratitude, through which people react to one another’s apparent goodwill or ill will.
Control shown when a person’s behavior is guided by their own psychological process, even if they could not have selected another option.
The capacity to recognize and respond appropriately to moral considerations. Some philosophers treat it as a condition of accountability.
Responsibility for an outcome that derives from responsibility for a related action, when the relevant causal and knowledge conditions are present.

questions_to_think_about: Does acting from one’s own reasons suffice for responsibility, even when one could not have acted otherwise?
Can blame be justified by beneficial effects if it is directed at someone who is not actually blameworthy?
Should a person’s upbringing affect how accountable they are for values they did not freely choose?
Is resentment best understood as an emotion, a moral protest, a demand, or several things at once?
If luck affects whether an attempt succeeds, should it affect blame for the result?

summaries.example: Jordan borrows a friend’s tablet and leaves it outside in the rain. In one version, Jordan knows rain is coming, could bring the tablet inside, and leaves it there because Jordan does not care. In another, Jordan is told the tablet is already broken and has no reason to expect rain. Jordan may be causally connected to the damage in both stories, but blame seems different. Philosophers would ask about Jordan’s knowledge, choices, control, reasons, and attitude toward the friend.
summaries.summary: Moral responsibility concerns when a person may fairly be praised, blamed, or held accountable for behavior. The entry distinguishes this from causal responsibility: causing an outcome does not automatically make someone morally responsible for it. A central debate asks what freedom requires. If determinism fixes every event through the past and the laws of nature, incompatibilists say the freedom needed for responsibility is impossible. Compatibilists reply that responsibility may require acting according to one’s choices without coercion, or having guidance control through a process that can respond to reasons. Other theories look forward to the effects of praise and blame, while the reactive-attitudes approach focuses on emotions such as resentment and gratitude and on whether an action shows regard or disregard for others. The entry also considers whether responsibility has different forms, whether moral understanding is necessary, whether blame is a kind of moral conversation, and whether one can be responsible for outcomes, omissions, or conduct shaped by luck and personal history. Philosophers disagree about how these parts fit together.
key_ideas: Moral responsibility is about the proper relationship between an agent and an action, not just about who caused an event.
Determinism says that the past and the laws of nature fix what happens. Incompatibilists see this as a threat to responsibility; compatibilists deny that it must be.
Some philosophers think a person can be responsible without having another option available, if the person’s own reasoning process guides the action.
Forward-looking accounts emphasize incentives and social benefits, while reactive-attitudes accounts emphasize relationships, respect, and emotional responses.
A person may be responsible in one sense because an action expresses their character, yet not accountable in another sense if blame would be unfair.
Ignorance, manipulation, upbringing, compulsion, and luck can all make responsibility harder to assess.
summaries.why_it_matters: Everyday judgments often move quickly from “this caused harm” to “this person deserves blame.” The philosophical discussion shows why that move needs care. A fair judgment may depend on what the person knew, intended, could control, and understood, as well as on how their history shaped them. These questions matter for deciding when to criticize, excuse, praise, apologize, repair damage, or change future behavior. They also help us examine whether our own practices are fair and whether they treat people as participants in moral relationships.

important_terms.definition: Being a suitable target of moral praise or blame for an action or result, because the action is connected to the person’s capacities and agency in the right way.
The ability to recognize relevant reasons and guide one’s behavior in response to them. Some theories use this instead of the ability to do otherwise.
A theory that explains responsibility practices partly by the good results they can produce, such as encouraging safer or kinder future behavior.
Feelings such as resentment, gratitude, and sometimes guilt that express how we respond to another person’s apparent goodwill or disregard.
A distinction between an action revealing morally important features of a person and that person being fairly subject to demands, criticism, or blame.
The ability to understand moral reasons and respond to them. Impairment of this ability may make blame unfair or pointless.
A situation in which factors outside a person’s control affect how they are morally judged, such as whether an intended harmful act succeeds.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between causing harm and deserving blame for harm?
Would a person be responsible if they acted from their own desires but those desires were created by manipulation?
Should moral blame require understanding the rule that was broken?
Can a useful blaming practice be justified even if responsibility is uncertain?
How much should luck matter when judging an attempt that succeeds or fails?
